summary:
Mexico has no single national procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none. Only seven states extend recognition to children. In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. A trans visitor's document position therefore depends on which state they are in.

Several states legislated recognition in their own right. Mexico City's Civil Code amendments allowing transgender people to change gender and name on birth certificates took effect on 13 March 2004. In late August 2008 the Legislative Assembly passed, by 37 to 17, a law formalising the procedure for changing names and obtaining revised birth certificates, replacing a prior process with no specific rules that could take years in court; on 13 November 2014 the Assembly approved a gender identity law making the process much quicker and simpler. The Michoacán Congress approved a gender identity law on 13 July 2017, Nayarit on 20 July 2017, Coahuila on 13 November 2018, Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosí began authorizing legal gender changes on 17 May 2019. The Supreme Court held on 17 October 2018 that a transgender person may change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity.

Where no procedure exists, identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

Tabasco had no legal gender-recognition procedure as of a Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report dated 6 March 2024. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The report set those findings against the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa, and against national figures showing that more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022. The report found trans people in Tabasco living without documents that match their gender.

Same-sex marriage is legal in every state. Mexico City's law of 21 December 2009 took effect on 4 March 2010 and was upheld 9-2 by the Supreme Court on 5 August 2010. On 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court released a jurisprudential thesis deeming laws restricting marriage to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring every judge to validate same-sex unions through amparo, with nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalised on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling, though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry in every state; adoption rights vary by state.

The constitutional and statutory anti-discrimination framework offers protection on paper. Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation on 2 September 1999, the first of its kind in the country. A federal anti-discrimination law took effect on 11 June 2003, creating a national council to enforce it. Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended in 2001 to prohibit discrimination under the term preferences, and in June 2011 the more precise term sexual orientation was inserted.
tangentialFactors:
Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatec Mayas, with Zapotecs recognising a traditional third gender known as muxe, intermediate between male and female. Muxes are assigned male at birth but typically act and behave like women and do both women's and men's work, and having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck and a blessing. The source states that muxes are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities, while recording that mestizos, especially mestizo police, occasionally harass and even persecute muxe boys and that Zapotec mothers and other women defend their right to be themselves.

Public LGBTQ visibility has a long documented history: visible and well-attended marches and pride parades have occurred in Mexico City since 1979, in Guadalajara since 1996, and in Monterrey since 2001.

The count of states operating a recognition procedure without legislative enactment, and the count of states extending recognition to children, are drawn from a March 2025 assessment; the inventory supplies no later state-level tally to compare it against.
localsOnly:
Residents of the six states whose legislatures enacted no recognition procedure, and of the two states operating one without enactment, depend on a process that state law does not codify. Only seven states extend recognition to children, although the Supreme Court extended the right to minors in 2022.

Residents whose identity documents do not match their gender face documented exclusion from employment, health services, education and financial transactions, and discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market; incidents of this kind are recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

Recourse machinery exists at two levels. Mexico City's 1999 ordinance banned discrimination based on sexual orientation, and the federal anti-discrimination law that took effect on 11 June 2003 created a national council to enforce it. Article 1 of the Federal Constitution has prohibited discrimination on the ground of preferences since 2001 and on the express ground of sexual orientation since June 2011.

Marriage is available to same-sex couples in every state, but adoption by those couples is permitted in only twenty states. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources date the Supreme Court's ruling on declaration-based name and gender-marker changes differently: one account gives 17 October 2017 and another 17 October 2018. The discrepancy is unresolved in this inventory.

The federal anti-discrimination law is dated 29 April 2003 in one account and recorded as taking effect on 11 June 2003 in another. Whether these are enactment and commencement dates respectively is not sourced here.

The incidents recorded in Guanajuato are undated in this inventory, so their recency cannot be established.

The 22-of-32 figure for states with a legislated procedure is a March 2025 snapshot. No later state-level tally is sourced, and no sourced account describes how the Supreme Court's 2022 guidelines have been enforced in the states that lack a procedure.

The figure of more than 95% of homicides going unpunished nationally in 2022 is a general homicide statistic. No trans-specific impunity figure is sourced, and the inventory supplies no denominator against which the documented trans killings can be ranked.
